title: Sesha Returns to the Ocean
subtitle: As Krishna watches, the great serpent issues from Balarama's mouth and the sea rises to receive him
story:
At Prabhasa the Yadava clans had destroyed themselves at last — brother falling on brother in a drunken quarrel, until the host that no enemy could break lay broken on the shore. The sea was quiet in the way of places where too much has happened. Krishna, who had watched his own clan destroy itself, went into the forest to find his elder brother, Balarama.

He had already set the aftermath in motion. Daruka, his charioteer, had been sent to the Kurus to summon Arjuna. Vabhru, a young chief of the clan, had been sent to guard the women of the house. Krishna had entered Dwaraka one last time, touched his father’s feet, and told him to protect the ladies until Arjuna came. Then he walked alone into the trees — and there he found Balarama.

His brother sat in a solitary spot, his back against the root of a tree, deep in meditation: the body still as the trunk behind it, the face turned inward. Krishna, coming upon him, saw at once that Balarama was not resting. He was leaving.

For even as Krishna watched, a great serpent began to issue from Balarama’s mouth. White as snow, huge as a mountain, crowned with a thousand hoods, red-eyed as fire, it slid out of the body it had dwelt in so long — out of the form of Balarama — and the forest seemed to hold its breath. This was Sesha, the thousand-headed serpent on whose coils Vishnu rests — the strength that had walked the earth as Krishna’s elder brother through every village game and every battle, returning now to its own nature.

The serpent did not linger. It went by the way that led to the ocean, moving with the unhurried certainty of something going home. And the ocean had heard.

For when Sesha reached the shore, the sea itself came forth to receive him. Ocean rose to meet the great naga, and with him came the kings of the serpents: Karkotaka, Vasuki and Takshaka; Prithusravas and Sankha; Kumuda and Pundarika; the high-souled Dhritarashtra, with Hrada and Kratha; Sitikantha, Chakramanda and Atishanda; Durmukha and Amvarisha. The sacred rivers came too, and Varuna, lord of the deep, at their head. They offered him the Arghya, the guest’s offering of honor, and water to wash his feet; they performed the rites of welcome and hailed him with the customary questions; saints and serpents hymned him together as the great white form passed into the waters and sank, and the deep closed over the thousand hoods without a ripple of violence.

Krishna stood in the forest and watched his brother’s essence enter the sea. What remained of Balarama sat where it was, a tree with its spirit departed; but the serpent that had been his other self was received by the ocean as a king returns to his kingdom, and the hush of the shore settled again.

Krishna wandered for a while in that lonely forest, thoughtful. He had known the end of all things before they came — Gandhari’s curse, the brahmins’ curse, the iron bolt, the quarrel at Prabhasa — and now, one after another, he recollected the words that had been spoken against his house, and the words of the sage Durvasas over the remnant of the payasa, the sweet milk-rice he had once eaten as Krishna’s guest. All of it had come to pass as it was said it would. His brother had gone before him, and the sea, which had been waiting, had taken what was its own. He sat down on the bare earth, and the forest kept watch around him.
reflection: Sesha's departure is Balarama's own — the strength that walked the earth as a brother returning to its original form, received not by death but by the ocean itself. Krishna watches without grief because there is nothing to grieve: what leaves the body here is not lost but welcomed home, and the sea that takes it in has been waiting.
tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana describes the scene briefly — the serpent issuing from Rama's mouth and entering the sea; the Mahabharata adds the long roll of serpent kings and sacred rivers who came to receive him.
next_story_tease: Before the end, the whole Yadava host had ridden out to Prabhasa in holiday spirits, unaware of what the shore held for them.
hero_scene: In a solitary clearing at Prabhasa, the white thousand-hooded serpent Sesha streams from the seated Balarama's mouth toward the sea, while Krishna stands watching, and beyond the trees the Ocean, ringed by serpent kings and sacred rivers, rises to receive him.
